## Introduction

Research and data science rarely happen in a single software ecosystem. You might pull data from a SQL database, receive spatial files from a GIS team, get genetic sequences from a lab, and need to hand your final analysis over to a colleague who only uses Excel or Python.

This workshop provides copy-pastable code to convert, import, and export data between R and almost any other format or software program in existence.

### 0. Setup: Installing the Ecosystem

Because we are covering everything from basic stats to bioinformatics and GIS, we need a robust set of tools from CRAN and Bioconductor.

```{r install-packages, eval=FALSE}
# 1. Standard CRAN Packages
cran_packages <- c(
  "rio", "haven", "readxl", "writexl", "R.matlab", # Stats & Tabular
  "DBI", "RSQLite",                                # Databases
  "jsonlite", "xml2",                              # Web & APIs
  "sf", "terra",                                   # Spatial / GIS
  "arrow", "reticulate",                           # Big Data & Python
  "magick",                                        # Images
  "pdftools", "readtext", "officer", "flextable"   # Word, PDF, Docs
)

new_cran <- cran_packages[!(cran_packages %in% installed.packages()[,"Package"])]
if(length(new_cran)) install.packages(new_cran, repos = "[http://cran.us.r-project.org](http://cran.us.r-project.org)")

# 2. Bioconductor Packages (for DNA/RNA seq and HDF5)
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager", repos = "[http://cran.us.r-project.org](http://cran.us.r-project.org)")
}
bioc_packages <- c("Biostrings", "rtracklayer", "rhdf5")
new_bioc <- bioc_packages[!(bioc_packages %in% installed.packages()[,"Package"])]
if(length(new_bioc)) BiocManager::install(new_bioc, update = FALSE, ask = FALSE)
library(tidyverse)
```

### 0.5 Generate Workshop Data (Run Once)

*Instructor Note: To ensure this script is entirely standalone, run this hidden chunk to generate the dummy files we will be importing in the following lessons.*

```{r generate-dummy-files, echo=FALSE, results='hide'}
# Create local directories
dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create("output", showWarnings = FALSE)

# 1. Tabular
rio::export(mtcars, "data/raw_data.csv")
rio::export(iris, "data/survey.xlsx")
rio::export(mtcars, "data/model_data.dta")
haven::write_sav(mtcars, "data/clinical.sav")
haven::write_xpt(mtcars, "data/legacy.xpt") # SAS Transport format

# 2. SQL Database
con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "data/company_database.sqlite")
DBI::dbWriteTable(con, "customers", mtcars, overwrite = TRUE)
DBI::dbDisconnect(con)

# 3. XML
xml2::write_xml(xml2::read_xml("<dataset><record><title>Workshop Data</title></record></dataset>"), "data/dataset.xml")

# 4. Spatial / GIS
dummy_sf <- sf::st_sf(id = 1, geometry = sf::st_sfc(sf::st_point(c(-73.9, 40.7))), crs = 4326)
sf::st_write(dummy_sf, "data/city_boundaries.shp", delete_dsn = TRUE, quiet = TRUE)

dummy_rast <- terra::rast(matrix(runif(100), 10, 10))
terra::writeRaster(dummy_rast, "data/elevation.tif", overwrite = TRUE)

# 5. Bioinformatics
Biostrings::writeXStringSet(Biostrings::DNAStringSet(c(Gene1="ATGCGT", Gene2="GGTACC")), "data/genome.fasta")
rtracklayer::export.bed(GenomicRanges::GRanges("chr1:100-200"), "data/peaks.bed")

# 6. MATLAB
R.matlab::writeMat("data/sensor_data.mat", my_matrix_name = matrix(1:9, 3, 3))

# 7. Unstructured Text (PDF)
pdf("data/report.pdf")
plot(1:10, main = "Automated Analysis Report", type="n")
text(5, 5, "This text was successfully extracted from the PDF.")
dev.off()

# 8. Images
img_blank <- magick::image_blank(100, 100, "lightblue")
magick::image_write(img_blank, "data/microscope_slide.tif")

# 9. Big Data (HDF5)
if(file.exists("data/single_cell.h5")) file.remove("data/single_cell.h5")
rhdf5::h5createFile("data/single_cell.h5")
rhdf5::h5createGroup("data/single_cell.h5", "matrix")
rhdf5::h5write(matrix(rnorm(100), 10, 10), "data/single_cell.h5", "matrix/data")

```

## 1. The "One-Stop Shop" for Tabular Data (`rio` & `haven`)

For standard spreadsheets and stats software (Excel, CSV, Stata, SPSS, SAS), the `rio` package acts as a universal translator. It reads the file extension and automatically uses the right package in the background.

```{r tabular-rio}
library(rio)
library(haven) # Loaded alongside rio to handle value labels

# ----- IMPORTING -----
df_csv   <- import("data/raw_data.csv")
df_excel <- import("data/survey.xlsx")
df_stata <- import("data/model_data.dta")
df_spss  <- import("data/clinical.sav")
df_sas   <- import("data/legacy.xpt")

# PRO TIP: Stata, SAS, and SPSS use "value labels" (e.g., 1 = Male, 2 = Female). 
# R uses "factors". Use haven::as_factor() to instantly convert them!
df_spss_clean <- as_factor(df_spss)

# ----- EXPORTING -----
export(df_csv, "output/for_colleague.xlsx")

# FIX: Stata doesn't allow periods in column names. 
# Replace periods (.) with underscores (_) before exporting
names(df_excel) <- gsub("\\.", "_", names(df_excel))

export(df_excel, "output/for_stata_users.dta")

# ----- DIRECT CONVERSION -----
# Convert a Stata file directly to Excel without even loading it into R memory!
convert("data/model_data.dta", "output/ready_for_excel.xlsx")

```

---

## 2. Databases & SQL

You don't need to export a database to a CSV to use it in R. You can query databases directly and bring the results in as an R data frame.

```{r databases}
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)

# Connect to a database (SQLite used here, but works for Postgres, MySQL, etc.)
con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "data/company_database.sqlite")

# See what tables exist in the database
dbListTables(con)

# Read an entire SQL table directly into an R data frame
df_customers <- dbReadTable(con, "customers")

# Write an R data frame back into the database as a new table
dbWriteTable(con, "cleaned_customers", df_customers, overwrite = TRUE)

# Always disconnect when done
dbDisconnect(con)

```

---

## 3. Web Data & APIs (JSON and XML)

Modern web APIs rarely send CSVs; they send JSON or XML. R handles these beautifully.

```{r web-json-xml}
library(jsonlite)
library(xml2)

# ----- JSON -----
# Import JSON from a local file or directly from a web API URL
api_url <- "https://api.github.com/users/hadley/repos"
df_json <- fromJSON(api_url) # Automatically flattens JSON into a data frame!

# Export R data frame to JSON (useful for web developers)
write_json(df_json, "output/data_for_web.json", pretty = TRUE)

# ----- XML -----
# Read XML data
xml_data <- read_xml("data/dataset.xml")
# Extract specific nodes using XPath
titles <- xml_find_all(xml_data, "//title") %>% xml_text()

```

---

## 4. Spatial Data & GIS (Maps)

Geospatial data usually comes in two flavors: **Vector** (points/polygons, like Shapefiles) and **Raster** (pixel grids, like GeoTIFF satellite imagery).

```{r spatial-gis}
library(sf)     # For Vector data
library(terra)  # For Raster data

# ----- VECTOR (Shapefiles, GeoJSON, KML) -----
# Import a shapefile or GeoJSON
map_vector <- st_read("data/city_boundaries.shp", quiet = TRUE)

# Export to GeoJSON (the modern web standard for maps)
st_write(map_vector, "output/web_map.geojson", delete_dsn = TRUE, quiet = TRUE)

# ----- RASTER (GeoTIFF, NetCDF) -----
# Import a satellite image or elevation model
map_raster <- rast("data/elevation.tif")

# Export raster data
writeRaster(map_raster, "output/processed_elevation.tif", overwrite = TRUE)

```

---

## 5. Bioinformatics: DNA, RNA, and Genomics

Bioinformatics heavily relies on specific file formats (FASTA, FASTQ, BED, GTF/GFF). We use Bioconductor packages to handle these without breaking R's memory.

```{r bioinformatics}
library(Biostrings)
library(rtracklayer)

# ----- SEQUENCE DATA (FASTA/FASTQ) -----
# Import DNA/RNA sequences (FASTA)
dna_seqs <- readDNAStringSet("data/genome.fasta")

# Export back to FASTA for use in other bioinformatics tools (like BLAST)
writeXStringSet(dna_seqs, "output/processed_sequences.fasta")

# ----- GENOMIC COORDINATES (BED/GTF) -----
# Import a BED file (genomic coordinates)
bed_data <- import.bed("data/peaks.bed")

# Export R genomic ranges to a BED file (e.g., to view in IGV browser)
export.bed(bed_data, "output/filtered_peaks.bed")

```

---

## 6. MATLAB and Matrix Data

MATLAB `.mat` files are hierarchical workspaces, not flat spreadsheets.

```{r matlab}
library(R.matlab)

# Import a MATLAB workspace (returns a list of objects)
mat_workspace <- readMat("data/sensor_data.mat")

# Extract a specific matrix from the MATLAB list and make it a data frame
r_dataframe <- as.data.frame(mat_workspace$my_matrix_name)

# Export an R matrix back to MATLAB
writeMat("output/r_matrices.mat", data_for_matlab = as.matrix(r_dataframe))

```

---

## 7. Unstructured Text: PDFs and Word Documents

Sometimes your data is trapped in reports, PDFs, or Word documents.

```{r text-docs}
library(pdftools)
library(officer)
library(flextable)

# ----- PDF -----
# Extract all text from a PDF (returns a character vector, 1 element per page)
pdf_text_data <- pdf_text("data/report.pdf")

# ----- MS WORD -----
# Create a new, blank Word document in R to send automated reports
my_doc <- read_docx() %>%
  body_add_par("Automated Analysis Report", style = "heading 1") %>%
  body_add_par("Here are the results from the R analysis.", style = "Normal") %>%
  body_add_flextable(flextable(head(mtcars))) # Add a neat table

# Save the document to your drive
print(my_doc, target = "output/automated_report.docx")

```

---

## 8. Images and Pixel Data

For computer vision or spatial transcriptomics, we can treat images as data arrays.

```{r images}
library(magick)

# Import an image (PNG, JPEG, TIFF, etc.)
img <- image_read("data/microscope_slide.tif")

# Export the processed image back to a file
image_write(img, path = "output/processed_slide.png", format = "png")

# Convert an image into a raw numeric array for statistical pixel analysis
# Note: We must use image_data() to extract the underlying tensor array first
pixel_array <- as.integer(image_data(img))

```

---

## 9. Big Data & Python Interoperability

When datasets exceed your computer's RAM, or when you need to seamlessly pass data to a Python collaborator, use **Parquet**, **HDF5**, and **Reticulate**.

### Arrow / Parquet & HDF5

```{r big-data}
library(arrow)
library(rhdf5)

# ----- ARROW/PARQUET (Massive Tabular Data) -----
# Export a massive R dataset to a compressed Parquet file
write_parquet(mtcars, "output/cloud_data.parquet")
# Import Parquet (loads infinitely faster than CSV)
huge_data <- read_parquet("output/cloud_data.parquet")

# ----- HDF5 (Massive Matrix Data / Single-Cell Genomics) -----
# Read a specific matrix out of an HDF5 file
expression_matrix <- h5read("data/single_cell.h5", name = "matrix/data")
# Write an R matrix into an HDF5 format
h5write(expression_matrix, file = "output/new_data.h5", name = "processed_matrix")

```

### Passing Data directly to Python (`reticulate`)

You don't even need to save a file to transfer data to Python! You can run Python *inside* RStudio and pass data back and forth in memory.

```{r reticulate-r-chunk}
library(reticulate)

# Let's say we have an R data frame
r_dataset <- mtcars

```

```{python reticulate-python-chunk}
# This is a Python chunk! We pull the R data frame using the 'r' object
import pandas as pd

# The r_dataset is automatically converted to a Pandas DataFrame
python_dataset = r.r_dataset

# Do some data manipulation in Python
python_dataset['mpg_doubled'] = python_dataset['mpg'] * 2

```

```{r back-to-r}
# Back in an R chunk, bring the modified Python data back to R using 'py'
final_r_dataset <- py$python_dataset

```
